orderFinding.conclusion: The order inside one update is AccessKit's and is not stable: three runs gave three different orders for the same three elements. On iOS, with no queue, each announcement interrupts the one before, so the user hears the last one asked for; an order that changes with the update would change which announcement is heard.
orderFinding.decision: One announcement per update, in the order asked for, a frame apart (commit 030ebcf).

decisions: An announcement is a new static text element under the FabricApplication's own element with the text as its value and a live mode, because AccessKit's macOS adapter speaks the value of a live node when it is added; a name alone is silent (measured), and Godot's own Window::accessibility_announcement uses the name.
Every announcement is an element of its own: a value equal to the one before does not speak again.

The element is made inside the accessibility update (NOTIFICATION_ACCESSIBILITY_UPDATE of the FabricApplication) and freed outside the update after it, because free_element is refused inside one; the free is followed by an update that takes the node out of the OS tree.
Priority 'high' is assertive; 'default', an absent or null priority and a string iOS ignores are polite. queue: true and priority 'low' are refused with the reason, as is the screen reader's focus.

With no screen reader (SceneTree.is_accessibility_enabled(), AccessibilityServer.is_supported() and an element for the application) the call returns and the announcement is counted and dropped; it is never kept for a screen reader that turns on later, and an announcement that waits more than 120 pumps for an update that does not come is dropped.
One announcement per update, in the order asked (commit 030ebcf): AccessKit posts the elements of one update in an order of its own, and on iOS the last announcement asked for is the one heard.

The announcements have a pure core of their own (native/accessibility_announcement_core.h, with its own test), independent of the settings' core, which includes it only because its Backend carries the announcements' port.

The validation seam is the application's validation_accessibility_announcer meta (available, element, delivers): a recorder replaces the AccessibilityServer, runs the update the engine would and records every call; the probe never sends the notification.
Every name the port calls is asked of the ClassDB once and reported in the snapshot (announcements.api); the oracle holds the names to its own list of Godot 4.7.2's.
announcementFinished stays silent: macOS, AccessKit and Godot have no end-of-speech signal, and Godot's text to speech is not the screen reader (it speaks without one), so it would invent the event.
The screen reader's focus is refused: Godot has one focus, and moving it is grab_focus(), which blurs a focused TextInput; iOS's UIAccessibilityLayoutChangedNotification does not.
limitations: Local macOS arm64 evidence; hosted CI and Pages are pending and recorded after the merge; other export targets are separate. The graphical lane needs a macOS window session and is not part of hosted CI.

That VoiceOver spoke an announcement is not proven by anything here: the lane proves what AccessKit asks AppKit to post (text, priority level, order, once each); the speech of a real VoiceOver is a manual check.
announcementFinished never fires (no end-of-speech signal anywhere in the stack).
queue: true and priority 'low' are refused: AppKit's announcement has no queue and AccessKit has only polite and assertive.
The screen reader's programmatic focus is refused (Godot has one focus); investigated: grab_focus() with FOCUS_ACCESSIBILITY and the virtual _get_focused_accessibility_element.

A View's accessibilityLiveRegion (the first slice) sets accessibility_live on a node with a name, not a value: by the adapter's code it is probably silent on macOS. Not measured on VoiceOver and not changed by this slice.
The order measured for the first design (three announcements of one frame in one update) is recorded from the round that found it; the code of that design is no longer in the tree.
The spike script is a local experiment, not versioned; its report and hashes are in this record.
Announcements hang from the FabricApplication's own element: two applications in one window announce to the same window, and a node with no element (window not visible) drops.
An announcement that waits for more pumps than 120 (a queue longer than that asked in one frame, or an update that never comes) is dropped.
Godot's mobile servers report no accessibility today; the iOS and Android bridges are GF-34 and GF-35. Windows and Linux AccessKit adapters were not measured.
In headless no real screen reader exists: the recorder stands in for the AccessibilityServer, and the real, headless server proves the drop path only.
